abstract: Neuronal cell types in the brain can show remarkable diversity in their functional properties. In the visual system, neurons at different levels of hierarchy show diverse kinetics, leading to the encoding of different features of the visual scene. How this behaviorally relevant diversification is achieved is not understood. Here, we address this question in a simple system, studying two visual cell types in Drosophila that diversify their responses despite receiving the same photoreceptor input to encode two distinct basic visual features, contrast and luminance. We first show that this cell type diversity is mostly established by cell-intrinsic mechanism. While cell-type specific transcriptome analysis delivers promising receptor and channel candidates, genetic manipulation of these differentially regulated genes fails to identify individual channels or receptors that are necessary or sufficient for the functional differences between luminance-sensitive L3 neurons and contrast-sensitive L2 neurons. However, loss of the L3-specific transcription factor dFezf makes L3 neurons transient and contrast-sensitive. Interestingly, dFezf controls the cell-type-specific expression of several receptors and ion channels that we initially found to be differentially expressed between L2 and L3. Together, this argues for a degenerate system in which multiple genes jointly shape cell type-specific functional properties. Our finding that a single transcription factor regulates the expression of such a set of genes that can be relevant for function suggest that similar regulation might also be in place in other degenerate systems, which exist widely across cell types, brain regions, and species.
